Dynamic diagram (deployment view): Partner amendment requests through SOAP to AWS validation.

Two external software systems sit outside every cloud boundary: Existing partner integrators and New partner integrators. Existing integrators call a Legacy SOAP API in Azure API Management (APIM); new integrators call a Partner SOAP API in the same APIM service. These are separate entry branches 1a and 1b, using SOAP over HTTPS and returning XML responses. Preserve both entry points.

Azure Cloud contains APIM and its two SOAP APIs, Azure AD B2C, Azure Cosmos DB for roles/permissions, and an Inbound processing software system boundary. Inbound processing contains API-Route-Processor and Common-Authx-Handler, both Logic Apps workflows, and a nested sub-workflows group containing Amend-Order-Processor and Amend-Document-Processor, also Logic Apps workflows. AWS Cloud contains API Gateway and a Core platform software system boundary containing Validation engine, an AWS Lambda function. An explicit site-to-site VPN joins the clouds; all stated Azure-to-AWS amend API traffic uses that connection.

APIM authenticates incoming requests against Azure AD B2C. The synthetic scenario specifies either basic or bearer authentication input; do not invent the token-exchange implementation or claim that Azure AD B2C natively exposes a Basic authentication protocol. APIM separately checks the system account's roles and the mandatory presence of a user profile for amend requests. It then passes the authenticated request to API-Route-Processor. API-Route-Processor delegates authorization to Common-Authx-Handler. The handler queries Cosmos DB using system account name and user profile name to check the required user-profile role. APIM's system-account role check and the handler's user-profile role check are distinct controls.

After authorization, routing is by method: amend_order goes to Amend-Order-Processor and requires ManageOrders; amend_document goes to Amend-Document-Processor and requires ManageDocuments. A user profile is mandatory for both amendment methods. Show this method-to-role mapping as a small architectural authorization table. There is no universal ManageOrders requirement for amend_document.

Each sub-workflow validates request XML, the method and malformed base64 content. It wraps decoded XML in JSON and calls the AWS amend API via API Gateway over the VPN using HTTPS/JSON. The exact AWS operation and response schema remain unspecified; preserve HTTPS/JSON without inventing an operation name or schema. API Gateway invokes Validation engine Lambda, which performs business-rule validation. The JSON response returns to the sub-workflow; the sub-workflow uses a Liquid template to convert JSON to XML, then returns the XML response through the SOAP entry path to the integrator. Fold normal responses into the corresponding request labels rather than drawing double-headed arrows.

Internal errors, such as an AWS-call timeout, are hidden from integrators; only a generic error response is returned. A separate failure response may use bold labels and caller-appropriate branches. Authentication and role queries are auxiliary/dashed; main forwarding is solid. Preserve the two entry branches and the method-specific sub-workflow routing, without inventing extra endpoints.

The source's cancel-order wording has been resolved to amend requests. Struck-out retrieval of accessible registrations and the orders-existence/accessibility query are deleted scope and must not appear. The contradictory universal ManageOrders sentence is superseded by the per-method table. No actual deployed identity exchange or API schema is asserted by this synthetic test input.

The diagram is titled “Dynamic diagram (deployment view): Partner amendment requests through SOAP to AWS validation.” Its stated purpose is to authenticate partner amendment requests, authorize the required user-profile role, validate in AWS, and return XML through the originating SOAP API.

Deployment and system membership

Two external software systems appear outside the cloud boundaries: Existing partner integrators and New partner integrators.

The Azure Cloud deployment node contains an Azure API Management (APIM) deployment node, an Inbound processing software-system boundary, Azure AD B2C, and a Roles / permissions store. Azure AD B2C is a container of type Identity provider. Roles / permissions is a container using Azure Cosmos DB. These two containers are outside both the APIM deployment node and the Inbound processing boundary, while remaining inside Azure Cloud.

The APIM deployment node contains three containers: Legacy SOAP API, of type SOAP API; Partner SOAP API, also of type SOAP API; and APIM policy processing, of type Azure API Management.

Inbound processing contains API-Route-Processor and Common-Authx-Handler, each a Logic Apps workflow container. It also contains a nested Sub-workflows software-system boundary. Sub-workflows contains two Logic Apps workflow containers: Amend-Order-Processor and Amend-Document-Processor. Thus four Logic Apps workflow containers are depicted in Azure.

A Site-to-site VPN container is shown between the Azure Cloud and AWS Cloud boundaries, outside both enclosing cloud boxes. Its type is “Azure ↔ AWS connection.”

The AWS Cloud deployment node contains an API Gateway container of type AWS API Gateway and a nested Core platform software-system boundary. Core platform contains a Validation engine container of type AWS Lambda function. API Gateway is inside AWS Cloud but outside Core platform.

Directed request flow and associated responses

The diagram numbers the flow and uses a/b suffixes to preserve caller or method branches. A solid single arrow means a request or forwarding action; its label also describes the normal response, rather than drawing a separate response arrow. A dashed single arrow denotes an auxiliary authentication or role query.

1a. Existing partner integrators initiate a SOAP over HTTPS request to Legacy SOAP API, crossing into Azure Cloud and the APIM deployment node. The response is XML.

1b. New partner integrators initiate a SOAP over HTTPS request to Partner SOAP API, crossing the same deployment boundaries. The response is XML.

2a. Legacy SOAP API forwards into APIM policy processing. The arrow is labeled “Enter APIM policy,” with XML as the request representation and an XML response.

2b. Partner SOAP API likewise forwards into APIM policy processing, labeled “Enter APIM policy,” with XML and an XML response. Both originating SOAP APIs therefore enter the same policy-processing container.

3. APIM policy processing initiates a dashed auxiliary “Authenticate” call to Azure AD B2C. Its qualifier is “[Identity]” and the response is labeled “Result.” This call leaves the APIM deployment node but stays within Azure Cloud. Authentication input may be basic or bearer. APIM authenticates against Azure AD B2C; the identity exchange implementation is explicitly unspecified.

APIM request controls apply after authentication: check system-account roles, and require a user profile for both amendment methods.

4. APIM policy processing sends an “Authenticated request after controls” to API-Route-Processor. The label specifies XML and an XML response. This crosses from the APIM deployment node into the Inbound processing software-system boundary, within Azure Cloud.

5. API-Route-Processor initiates a dashed “Delegate authorization” call to Common-Authx-Handler. It is a workflow call and returns a role decision.

6. Common-Authx-Handler initiates a dashed query to Roles / permissions in Azure Cosmos DB. The query supplies “system account name + user profile name” and returns the “Required user-profile role result.” It crosses out of Inbound processing while remaining inside Azure Cloud.

7a. API-Route-Processor calls Amend-Order-Processor inside the nested Sub-workflows boundary for the amend_order method. This workflow call requires ManageOrders and returns XML.

7b. API-Route-Processor calls Amend-Document-Processor inside Sub-workflows for the amend_document method. This workflow call requires ManageDocuments and returns XML.

8a. Amend-Order-Processor initiates an “AWS amend API” call toward the Site-to-site VPN, with HTTPS/JSON and a JSON response. This leaves the Sub-workflows and Inbound processing boundaries and Azure Cloud.

8b. Amend-Document-Processor initiates the corresponding “AWS amend API” call toward the same Site-to-site VPN, also using HTTPS/JSON with a JSON response and leaving those Azure boundaries.

9a and 9b. The VPN forwards the respective branches as “Traffic routing” to the single API Gateway in AWS Cloud. Both labels specify HTTPS/JSON and a JSON response. These routes enter the AWS Cloud boundary.

10. API Gateway initiates an “Invoke” call to the Validation engine inside Core platform. The call is qualified as “Lambda invocation” and returns a JSON response.

Processing, authorization, and failure requirements

Both sub-workflows validate XML, the method, and malformed base64. They wrap decoded XML in JSON. Their response transformation is explicitly “JSON response → Liquid template → XML.” They return XML through the originating SOAP API.

The method-authorization table states that amend_order requires the user-profile role ManageOrders, with a mandatory user profile. It states that amend_document requires the user-profile role ManageDocuments, also with a mandatory user profile. APIM system-account role checks and Common-Authx-Handler user-profile role checks are distinct controls. No explicit denial status, denial payload, or separate denial route is shown for a failed role check or missing profile.

Failure handling hides internal errors, with an AWS-call timeout given as an example. Only a generic error response is returned through the originating SOAP entry: Legacy SOAP API returns to existing integrators, and Partner SOAP API returns to new integrators. The generic error's exact schema or status is not specified.

The AWS amend operation and response schema are explicitly unspecified. The Validation engine applies business-rule validation. The diagram does not specify the individual business rules, call frequency, or an identity-exchange implementation.

The legend identifies the service icons as official Azure2 / AWS4 catalog entries and says that boundaries represent deployment or software-system domains. No additional behavior is implied by icon placement or by line routing beyond the labeled calls and boundary crossings.

An Azure Cloud deployment node contains an Azure API Management (APIM) deployment node, Azure AD B2C (a container and identity provider), a Roles / permissions container using Azure Cosmos DB, and an Inbound processing software-system boundary. The APIM deployment node contains Legacy SOAP API and Partner SOAP API, both containers of type SOAP API, and APIM policy processing, a container using Azure API Management. The Inbound processing boundary contains API-Route-Processor and Common-Authx-Handler, both Azure Logic Apps workflow containers, plus a nested “Sub-workflows — 2 workflows” software-system boundary containing Amend-Order-Processor and Amend-Document-Processor, also Azure Logic Apps workflow containers. Four Azure Logic Apps workflow containers are depicted in total.

Outside Azure Cloud are two external software systems: Existing partner integrators and New partner integrators. A Site-to-site VPN container, labeled “Azure ↔ AWS connection,” is outside the depicted Azure and AWS cloud boundaries and connects the Azure workflows to AWS. An AWS Cloud deployment node contains an API Gateway container using AWS API Gateway and a nested Core platform software-system boundary. That Core platform boundary contains Validation engine, an AWS Lambda function container responsible for business-rule validation. API Gateway is within AWS Cloud but outside the Core platform boundary.

The numbered directed requests and their response annotations are:

1a. Existing partner integrators initiate SOAP over HTTPS to Legacy SOAP API, crossing into Azure Cloud and APIM. The response is XML.
1b. New partner integrators initiate SOAP over HTTPS to Partner SOAP API, crossing into Azure Cloud and APIM. The response is XML.
2a. Legacy SOAP API enters APIM policy processing with XML. The response is XML.
2b. Partner SOAP API enters APIM policy processing with XML. The response is XML.
3. APIM policy processing initiates “Authenticate [Identity]” against Azure AD B2C, across the APIM deployment boundary but within Azure Cloud. The return annotation is “Result.” Authentication input may be basic or bearer. APIM authenticates against Azure AD B2C; the identity exchange implementation is unspecified.
4. APIM policy processing forwards an “Authenticated request after controls” to API-Route-Processor, crossing from APIM into the Inbound processing boundary. The request is XML and the response is XML.
5. API-Route-Processor delegates authorization to Common-Authx-Handler through a workflow call. The response is a role decision.
6. Common-Authx-Handler queries Azure Cosmos DB, crossing out of the Inbound processing boundary while staying within Azure Cloud. The query supplies “system account name + user profile name”; the response is the required user-profile role result.
7a. API-Route-Processor calls Amend-Order-Processor for amend_order through a workflow call, entering the nested sub-workflows boundary. This method requires ManageOrders. The response is XML.
7b. API-Route-Processor calls Amend-Document-Processor for amend_document through a workflow call, entering the nested sub-workflows boundary. This method requires ManageDocuments. The response is XML.
8a. Amend-Order-Processor calls the AWS amend API over HTTPS/JSON via the Site-to-site VPN, leaving the sub-workflows, Inbound processing, and Azure Cloud boundaries. The response is JSON.
8b. Amend-Document-Processor calls the AWS amend API over HTTPS/JSON via the Site-to-site VPN, likewise leaving those Azure boundaries. The response is JSON.
9a and 9b. The Site-to-site VPN routes each workflow's traffic to API Gateway inside AWS Cloud, over HTTPS/JSON. Each response is JSON.
10. API Gateway invokes Validation engine across the Core platform boundary using “Lambda invocation.” The response is JSON.

APIM controls after authentication check system-account roles and require a user profile for both amendment methods. Common-Authx-Handler checks the user-profile role; this is distinct from APIM's system-account role checks. The method authorization table specifies that amend_order requires user-profile role ManageOrders and a mandatory user profile, while amend_document requires user-profile role ManageDocuments and a mandatory user profile. For a failed role check or missing profile, no explicit denial status, payload, or separate denial route is shown.

Both sub-workflows validate XML, method, and malformed base64. They wrap decoded XML in JSON. Their JSON response is transformed through a Liquid template into XML, and they return XML through the originating SOAP API.

Failure handling hides internal errors, for example an AWS-call timeout. Only a generic error is returned through the originating SOAP entry: Legacy for existing integrators, Partner for new integrators. The exact error schema and status are unspecified.

The AWS amend operation and response schema are unspecified. Individual business rules and call frequency are unspecified.

The legend identifies official Azure2 / AWS4 catalog service icons and plain boxes where a service icon is inapplicable. Boundaries represent deployment or software-system domains. A solid filled arrow denotes a request or forwarding action; a dashed filled arrow denotes auxiliary authentication or a role query. Normal responses are folded into request labels rather than drawn as separate response paths. VPN legs are traffic routing. No additional behavior is implied by icon placement or line routing.

judgeNotes: Atomic propositions are assigned to a single dimension; directed relationships carry their call direction rather than duplicating that information in the directions dimension. Compound sentences are split where they assert different responsibilities or controls. Shared memberships and repeated branch protocols are grouped only when semantically identical.

Source authoring instructions, deleted scope, superseded universal ManageOrders wording, synthetic-test caveats, diagram presentation instructions, titles, legends and icon catalog choices are excluded from architecture facts. The prohibition on inventing token exchange is not extracted as a system proposition. L2/L4 explicitly keeping that implementation unspecified adds no implementation or real-system constraint, and their readout-only identity-implementation absence is likewise excluded.

C4 type/technology annotations, count summaries of the same four workflows, the connection representation for the VPN and policy-processing representation of the same APIM service are accepted as faithful notation. No separate APIM hosting/lifecycle or third SOAP endpoint is asserted. The nested Sub-workflows software-system label is treated as a grouping of the same two existing workflows inside the same Inbound owner, with no independent owner or lifecycle asserted.

Readout-only absences about denial payloads/status/routes, business-rule lists, call frequency, and exact generic error schemas are not new system facts. Their absence does not prove an allow/deny outcome or a real-system constraint. No unstated vendor behavior is inferred.

L4 describes the integrators as external software systems outside Azure; its whole topology places AWS elsewhere and gives them only Azure entry branches. I read this as the same external actors, not newly AWS-owned integrators. VPN placement outside boxes expresses a cross-cloud connection without changing its owner.

Workflow-call and Lambda-invocation labels describe already-stated calls to workflows and a Lambda. XML on the within-APIM / APIM-forwarding path and role-decision/result labels faithfully elaborate the source XML request/response and authorization flow. The one distinct extra payload assertion is JSON on the internal Lambda response, separated from the source JSON response returned to each sub-workflow.

No explicit denial behavior is inferred from mandatory-profile and role prerequisites. Authorization-first sequencing remains in the numbered query-then-routing flow. Both method-role mappings remain distinct and no universal ManageOrders control is asserted.
